name: Isoniazid
mechanism: Prodrug activated by mycobacterial catalase-peroxidase (katG). Active form inhibits InhA enzyme (enoyl-acyl carrier protein reductase), blocking mycolic acid synthesis → disrupts mycobacterial cell wall. Bactericidal against actively dividing M. tuberculosis. Most potent single TB drug
dosing: Standard regimen: 300mg PO OD (5mg/kg, max 300mg) or 15mg/kg 3x/week (max 900mg, DOT). Part of RIPE regimen (Rifampicin, Isoniazid, Pyrazinamide, Ethambutol) for 2 months intensive phase, then RIF+INH for 4 months continuation (total 6 months). Latent TB: 300mg OD for 6 months, or 900mg 2x/week (DOT) for 9 months. Paediatric: 10mg/kg OD (max 300mg). ALWAYS give pyridoxine 10-25mg daily (prevents peripheral neuropathy)
contraindications: Acute liver disease, drug-induced hepatitis (previous isoniazid). Caution: chronic liver disease, alcohol excess, HIV (higher hepatotoxicity), diabetes (monitor), renal impairment (dosing unchanged, but increased toxicity risk), epilepsy (may lower seizure threshold), porphyria
interactions: Rifampicin: additive hepatotoxicity (but used together in TB regimens - monitor LFTs closely). Phenytoin: isoniazid inhibits metabolism → ↑ phenytoin levels (toxicity - monitor levels). Carbamazepine: similar interaction. Alcohol: ↑ hepatotoxicity. Paracetamol: theoretical ↑ hepatotoxicity. Antacids: ↓ isoniazid absorption (separate by 2h). Tyramine-containing foods (cheese, wine): isoniazid weak MAOI - may cause hypertensive reaction (rare)
monitoring: LFTs at baseline, then monthly (or 2-weekly in first 2 months, higher risk). Stop if ALT >5× ULN (or >3× if symptomatic), or clinical hepatitis. Signs of hepatotoxicity (jaundice, N&V, abdominal pain, fatigue - advise patients to report immediately). Peripheral neuropathy symptoms (tingling, numbness - preventable with pyridoxine). Visual acuity (if on ethambutol concurrently). Adherence (DOT recommended). Culture/sensitivity. HIV status. FBC (rare haematological effects)
pregnancy: USE if indicated - untreated TB greater risk to mother/fetus than treatment. Isoniazid safe in pregnancy (WHO/NICE recommend). ESSENTIAL: give pyridoxine 25mg daily (higher dose in pregnancy - prevents neonatal neuropathy). Monitor LFTs (physiological changes in pregnancy)
sideEffects: Common: hepatotoxicity (10-20% transient LFT ↑, 1% clinical hepatitis, 0.1% fatal hepatic necrosis - risk factors: age >35, alcohol, hepatitis B/C, HIV, concurrent hepatotoxic drugs). Peripheral neuropathy (dose-related, 10-20% without pyridoxine, <1% with pyridoxine - ALWAYS co-prescribe). Rash, fever (hypersensitivity). Uncommon: CNS effects (dizziness, seizures - lowers threshold, psychosis), optic neuritis (rare, unlike ethambutol), arthralgia, SLE-like syndrome, haematological (agranulocytosis, aplastic anaemia - rare). Drug-induced lupus. Pellagra (niacin deficiency - rare, high-dose therapy)
pharmacokinetics: Well absorbed orally (food ↓ absorption - take on empty stomach). Peak 1-2h. Widely distributed, including CSF (good for TB meningitis). Metabolized by N-acetylation (genetic polymorphism - fast/slow acetylators). Slow acetylators: higher drug levels, increased hepatotoxicity/neuropathy risk. Fast acetylators: lower levels, but usually adequate. Half-life: 1-4h (slow acetylators), 0.5-1.5h (fast acetylators). Excreted in urine (metabolites)
clinicalPearls: MOST POTENT single TB drug. Cornerstone of TB treatment. Part of standard 6-month regimen (2 months RIPE, then 4 months RI). Also used for latent TB (6-9 months monotherapy). PYRIDOXINE: ALWAYS co-prescribe 10-25mg daily (prevents peripheral neuropathy - B6 deficiency from isoniazid-induced increased excretion). Higher dose (25mg) if diabetes, HIV, alcoholism, malnutrition, pregnancy. HEPATOTOXICITY: most concerning side effect. RISK FACTORS: age >35, alcohol, hepatitis, HIV, first 2 months of therapy. BLACK BOX WARNING: severe/fatal hepatitis possible. Educate patients: stop immediately if jaundice, N&V, abdominal pain, dark urine - seek urgent review. Monthly LFTs. Stop if ALT >5× ULN or symptomatic. If hepatitis develops, usually in first 3 months. RESTART cautiously once resolved (specialist advice - may need alternative regimen). Slow acetylators: ~50% White/Black populations, ~10% Asian. Higher toxicity risk but usually clinically insignificant (standard dosing adequate). DRUG INTERACTIONS: inhibits CYP2C19/3A4 (weak) - main interaction phenytoin (monitor levels). DOT (directly observed therapy) recommended - ensures adherence. Resistance: katG mutation common mechanism (loss of activation). If resistance suspected, add second-line drugs (fluoroquinolone, aminoglycoside). CNS penetration good - used in TB meningitis (often higher dose 10mg/kg, max 600mg in severe CNS disease). Take on empty stomach (food ↓ absorption). ALTERNATIVES if intolerant: rifampicin + ethambutol + pyrazinamide (but less effective without isoniazid). Latent TB: isoniazid 6 months, or rifampicin 3-4 months, or RI 3 months (more convenient, better tolerated). Breastfeeding: safe (small amounts in milk, continue pyridoxine in infant)
indication: Active tuberculosis (pulmonary and extrapulmonary) as part of standard multi-drug regimen. Latent TB infection (treatment to prevent progression to active disease)
